{"id":"gen-1794669262-Yp8aQjBorvU2NcA3L1XQ","object":"chat.completion","created":1794669262,"model":"deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017","provider":"River","system_fingerprint":null,"service_tier":null,"choices":[{"index":0,"logprobs":null,"finish_reason":"stop","native_finish_reason":"stop","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"{
  "rating": 0.45,
  "explanation": "The operative regime is split and the harshest rule governs the traveller's journey stages. At the border, national rules bar new X-markers, direct officers to refuse where documents cast doubt on sex, and raise a material-misrepresentation finding carrying lifetime ineligibility; neighbouring governments have issued advisories after detentions. National facilities rules exclude trans people from sex-congruent single-sex facilities in federally funded settings, and immigration custody carries documented beatings, forced labour and sexual abuse. The division, by contrast, has codified gender-identity non-discrimination, explicit hate-crime coverage, a panic-defence ban and working courts. Those protections operate in hotels, clinics and local policing but do not pre-empt federal entry screening, federal facilities or federal custody, so they raise the local sphere without cancelling the tier-1 federal exposures.",
  "factor_matrix": {
    "entry_documents": {
      "exposure": "National rules bar new X-markers; officers must refuse cases where records cast doubt on sex and may consider a material-misrepresentation finding carrying permanent ineligibility. Passports reported confiscated; regional governments issued advisories after detentions.",
      "protection": "Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; policy is under litigation; legal-aid FAQ exists.",
      "interaction": "Division protections do not reach federal border adjudication; a document mismatch escalates into a federal fraud inquiry.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "investigation_detention_custody": {
      "exposure": "Immigration custody: trans men report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; corrections bureau adopted conversion-therapy-style practices and stopped reporting trans prisoner numbers.",
      "protection": "None documented reaching federal immigration or corrections custody.",
      "interaction": "A border document discrepancy can convert a visitor into a detainee subject to the federal custody regime, not the division's.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "federal_state_facilities": {
      "exposure": "National order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; many divisions ban such access in government buildings, one arrest documented elsewhere.",
      "protection": "Division is rated low-risk with no documented local facilities ban; local civil-rights act covers gender identity in services.",
      "interaction": "Federal buildings, airports and federally funded sites follow the national rule; private and division venues follow the protective local law.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "care_services": {
      "exposure": "National measures target youth gender-affirming care and reimbursement; federal funding freeze; adult visitor's own maintenance medication is not directly restricted in the dossier.",
      "protection": "Division bans conversion therapy and bars insurer discrimination on gender identity.",
      "interaction": "Federal health rules affect federally funded programmes; division-regulated insurance and providers remain protective.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "threat_framing_law_enforcement": {
      "exposure": "Counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups for prioritised neutralisation; reward memorandum references 'radical gender ideology' but not as a reward criterion.",
      "protection": "The strategy states powers will not target people who simply disagree; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity.",
      "interaction": "Rhetoric raises climate severity but no documented enforcement action against trans visitors; local police operate under division civil-rights law.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "minors_guardians": {
      "exposure": "National order frames youth care as mutilation and directs investigation of schools facilitating social transition; 27 divisions ban youth care; subpoenas for patient records.",
      "protection": "Division bans conversion therapy and prohibits gender-identity discrimination, including by insurers.",
      "interaction": "A trans minor travelling with a guardian faces border document scrutiny and federal care restrictions; division services remain lawful and protective.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "street_violence_police_response": {
      "exposure": "No division-specific anti-trans violence data in the dossier; national bias-crime statistics do not isolate gender identity.",
      "protection": "Division hate-crime statute covers gender identity explicitly from 2025; panic defence abolished; civil-rights commission exists; courts have ruled for trans claimants.",
      "interaction": "Local police and prosecutors have operative tools; federal rhetoric may chill reporting.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "remedies_unknowns": {
      "exposure": "Federal measures are contested and status varies by date; a traveller may meet a rule in force one week and enjoined the next.",
      "protection": "Litigation ongoing; division courts demonstrably grant relief; legal-aid guidance exists.",
      "interaction": "Remedies work at division level; no documented remedy for a federal border or custody decision.",
      "status": "documented"
    }
  },

    {
      "anchor_id": "0.35-A",
      "comparison": "That anchor ends in release with an ombudsman citing a fairness charter and only residual uncertainty. Here entry refusal and a possible lifetime fraud finding are documented national practice, with custody harm behind it; local protections are stronger, but they do not reach the border desk, so this sits above that anchor's risk."

      "comparison": "That anchor's policy functioned: care was delivered after a supervisor intervened, with only friction remaining. Here the division's protections likewise function locally, but the federal exposures at entry, facilities and custody have no documented working remedy, so this rates materially below."
    },
    {
      "anchor_id": "0.85-C",

  "synthesis": "A trans visitor meets two regimes in sequence. The division is genuinely protective — codified non-discrimination, explicit hate-crime coverage, no conversion therapy, courts that have granted relief — so hotels, clinics, private venues and local police are comparatively low-risk. But the journey passes through federal hands first: document screening where a mismatch invites refusal and a possible permanent misrepresentation finding, facilities exclusion in federally funded buildings, and a custody regime with documented abuse. Division law does not pre-empt those actors, so the protective local layer cannot offset the federal exposure, and the overall rating stays below the midpoint."
}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"Let me work through the combined regime: parent national framework is highly hostile at the federal level (passport marker restrictions, entry screening with fraud/ineligibility findings, facility access restrictions federally funded, custody harm documented, threat-framing of "radically pro-transgender" groups). The division (state/province) is protective: non-discrimination codified, conversion therapy ban, hate crime with gender identity, panic defence abolished, marker change possible on birth certificate, low-risk tier on legal risk map.

Key visitor exposures:
- Entry/documents: federal executive order; passports with X markers not processed; officers instructed to refuse where discrepancy casts doubt on sex; potential material misrepresentation → permanent lifetime ineligibility. This is a documented traveller-facing exposure — universal at the border for trans travellers with mismatched markers. Detentions of citizens from a neighbouring jurisdiction over visa issues have occurred; governments issued advisories.
- Federal facilities: federal funding barred for single-sex facilities congruent with identity; state/province bans on facilities in 55+ states — but the division itself appears to be in the low-risk tier and not among the ban states (unspecified). However federal facilities (airports, federal buildings) apply the federal rule.
- Custody: documented harm in immigration custody (forced labour, sexual abuse, beatings), corrections conversion-therapy practice for inmates.
- Care services: state/province is protective but noted shortfall on healthcare equity; federal measures target youth care.
- Threat framing: counterterrorism strategy language — but explicitly "will not be used to target people who simply disagree"; the reward memo never uses radical gender ideology as criterion. So it's climate, not a direct targeting lever.
- Street violence: no state-specific data; national hate crime statute covers gender identity; state hate crime explicit post-2025.
- Remedies: state civil rights act, commission, courts working (2022 ruling, codified protections) — genuine operative protections at division level, plus federal hate crime statute. Some recourse working FOR trans people.
- Minors: travelling with a minor — federal EO directs investigation/prosecution of teachers, care bans in 27 states; in this division conversion therapy banned, but federal care restrictions and the "mutilation" framing create risk for a trans minor; care access for minors uncertain. Border entry of a trans minor with parent — document discrepancy exposure.

Now the combined regime: no criminalisation of trans identity per se; no sodomy enforcement (national 2003 ruling; statute unrepealed but dead letter). The harshest operative rule the traveller experiences: federal border document screening where discrepancy → refusal, potential lifetime ineligibility finding, possible detention; federal facilities exclusion; immigration custody harm. But division has robust protections and low-risk rating.

Where does this sit? Compare anchors. The rubric: 0.55 tier = protection works but public friction/uncertainty. 0.65 = protections generally work with friction. 0.75 = protection works smoothly with residual unknowns. 0.35-0.45 = denial of entry without detention, service denial.

Here: entry is a genuine risk — denial of entry is plausible for a trans traveller whose documents are flagged; detention possible; federal facilities exclusion universal; but for a traveller whose documents match (passport issued M/F consistent with presentation), most of this doesn't trigger. Important: rate what happens if outed. If outed at the border, refusal, potential lifetime ineligibility fraud finding — severity 3 (denial of entry/stranding). Federal facility exclusion — tier 1 universal exposure, since federal law bars trans people from single-sex facilities congruent with identity in federally funded settings. That's a documented state-imposed universal exposure. Custody harm in immigration detention — tier 1/2, severe.

So combined: the division's protections do not cancel federal entry screening, federal facilities, federal custody. Per rule, "A state's public-accommodation, health-care, or equality law does not cancel federal entry screening, federal facilities, federal prosecution, federal detention, federal custody."

But severity: no execution, no imprisonment for being trans per se; identity fraud finding is civil immigration ineligibility, not imprisonment. Detention in immigration custody carries documented abuse. Street violence baseline unclear; no state-specific data; general tolerance unclear (66% support for birth-sex markers = social friction/hostility moderate).

I'd place this around 0.40-0.50. The division is genuinely protective: robust non-discrimination, hate crime, working courts (a positive of the "remedy working" kind for the local sphere), but those don't reach the border or federal custody. Entry exposure is documented and traveller-facing (advisories from 8 governments, detentions of neighbouring citizens). Federal facility exclusions are universal exposure.

I think ~0.42-0.48. Let me pick 0.45. Compare to anchor 0.45-A/B: denial of entry, no detention, open questions, thin remedies — that's the entry profile here actually. But here we add documented detention harm in immigration custody and federal facility exclusion. Conversely we have stronger local protections than those anchors' jurisdictions.

Hmm, the anchors at 0.45 involve service denial and exclusion, no criminalisation, weak remedies. Here entry risk is roughly at that level or somewhat worse (possible lifetime ineligibility, documented detentions of travellers), plus federal custody abuse risk documented (immigration custody), plus threat-framing climate. Local sphere is better than 0.45 anchors.

The traveller's exposure concentrates at the border and in federal institutions — where the harsh rules operate. The division's protections govern hotels, restaurants, local police, local services — but local police here are the division's and do enforce civil rights (state hate crime, commission). That's real.

I'll go 0.42. That's Elevated Risk, near lower end. Hmm, let me consider 0.45 vs 0.40.

Factors weighing down: entry document screening with fraud/lifetime bar; facility exclusion in federally funded settings; immigration custody abuse documented; social opinion 66% support birth-sex marker laws (hostility-ish, though it's a policy-poll).

Weighing up: division-level protections documented and operating (court rulings, codified law, hate crime effective Jan 2025, panic defence abolished); no criminalisation; no sodomy enforcement; national hate crime statute; legal-aid FAQ infrastructure; state rated low-risk.

I think 0.45 is defensible. Actually, note that the entry exposure applies massively to a traveller whose passport marker mismatches presentation: "where there is a discrepancy in an applicant's documents or records... refuse the case and request additional evidence." That's for visa applicants mainly (cable instructs posts). Travellers from visa-waiver countries arriving with existing valid passports — X-marker passports remain valid until expiry. So the entry friction is real but not universal for all trans visitors; it bites visa applicants and those flagged.

Given that, a plausible score a bit above 0.45: maybe 0.48. But federal facilities exclusion is universal for outed travellers (tier 1). Hmm — the federal EO bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity. That's a genuine tier-1 universal exposure for outed trans visitors using federal buildings (airports, national parks, federal courthouses). Combined with the border exposure, I'd keep it below 0.5. Let's say 0.44.

I'll settle at 0.45 — Elevated, reflecting documented traveller-facing border/facility/custody exposures partially offset by unusually strong division-level protections that operate locally but do not reach federal actors.

Anchor checks: 0.35-A (ombudsman release, protections functioning), 0.45-A (denial of entry with registry flag, no detention, weak remedies), 0.55-D or 0.65-A (protection functions despite friction), and maybe 0.75-C. Need three different IDs. Use 0.35-A, 0.45-A, 0.65-B, maybe 0.75-C.
